name: Marrakech
tagline: Rose-red ramparts, palm gardens and the artisan's hand.
bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: Spring and autumn are the season, mild days for gardens and riads; time it to the December film festival or the May rose harvest, and avoid the July-August furnace.

ourTake.lede: A riad inside the medina is the only way to understand the city, thick walls, a still courtyard, and the souks a two-minute walk from your door. Do the Jemaa el-Fnaa at dusk when the food stalls light up, not in the flat midday heat, and give the snake charmers a wide berth. Balance the medina's intensity with a day at a garden or a palmeraie estate; the contrast is the pleasure of the place.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a riad courtyard, a hammam, and the theatre of the medina within an easy flight of an Atlas Mountains escape.
ourTake.skipIf: You need a beach holiday or expect a polished, sanitised city; the souks are intense and the hustle is real.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Royal Mansour Marrakech
credentials: World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 13, Best Hotel in Africa)
The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The King's own house, 53 private riads, each a world, and North Africa at its most complete.

items.name: La Mamounia
credentials: Travel + Leisure World's Best Awards 2025 (Hall of Fame)
Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice 2025, No. 1 Hotel in Africa
items.description: The grande dame since 1923, twelve hectares of walled gardens and the address every visit is measured against.

items.name: The Oberoi Marrakech
credentials: Travel + Leisure, Editor's Choice, Best International Leisure Hotel 2025
Condé Nast Traveler, Top 15 Hotels in Africa 2025
World Travel Awards, Morocco's Leading Luxury Hotel 2024
items.description: An Andalusian-Moroccan palace in a 28-acre olive grove, the surest, most Indian-fluent hands in the city.

items.name: Amanjena
items.description: Ed Tuttle's serene ochre pavilions around a reflecting basin, Aman calm, a world from the souk's noise.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Marrakech
items.description: Fifty acres of olive groves and rose gardens, and villas with their own pools, the group's precision, unhurried.

items.name: Four Seasons Resort Marrakech
items.description: A palace-scaled resort in forty acres of gardens, the Four Seasons default when nothing should go wrong.

items.name: Fairmont Royal Palm Marrakech
items.description: A golf-and-Atlas retreat on 231 hectares, the snow-capped mountains filling every terrace.

items.name: Selman Marrakech
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: Jacques Garcia drama and a stable of Arabian thoroughbreds beside a 80-metre pool, theatre, done with taste.

items.name: Kasbah Tamadot
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice 2025, No. 5 Hotel in Africa
items.description: Richard Branson's mountain kasbah above the Atlas valleys, the great escape from the city, into the peaks.

items.name: Nobu Hotel Marrakech
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: Moroccan craft meets Japanese cool, an all-suite house in the 'golden triangle', with the Nobu you know downstairs.

items.name: La Villa des Orangers
items.description: A former pasha's palace turned Relais & Châteaux riad, orange-tree patios, three pools, five minutes from the great square.

items.name: La Sultana Marrakech
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A jewel-box of five joined riads in the Kasbah, carved cedar, a heated pool and a roof over the royal quarter.

items.name: La Maison Arabe
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: Morocco's first boutique riad, opened 1946, Churchill's Marrakech, kept with quiet grace.

items.name: El Fenn
items.description: A riotously art-filled riad of plunge pools and colour, moments from Jemaa el-Fnaa, the bohemian heart of the Medina.

items.name: L'Hôtel Marrakech
items.description: Jasper Conran's five-suite riad, Diana's favourite designer, and his eye on every cushion and courtyard.

items.name: Farasha Farmhouse
items.description: A restored farmhouse on a plateau between two mountain ranges, a place built to slow the pulse right down.

items.name: Riad Sakkan
items.description: Two 17th-century riads joined into one, a vibrant, funky boutique house with a bar and kitchen of its own.

items.name: Riad Kheirredine
items.description: An intimate, romantic riad of carved rooms and a rooftop over the Medina, a heated pool at its centre.

items.name: Dar Zemora
items.description: A garden villa-hotel in the palm groves, walled, green and blessedly quiet, with the city minutes away.

items.name: Beldi Country Club
items.description: A rose-scented country estate of gardens, pools and its own workshops, the anti-resort, ten minutes from the walls.

items.name: Jemaa el-Fnaa
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Medina of Marrakesh
UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity
items.description: The city's great open-air theatre, storytellers, snake charmers, orange-juice carts and night-time food stalls filling a vast square as the Koutoubia lights up behind it. Best watched at dusk with tea from a rooftop terrace above the fray, an easy, safe first evening for a multi-generational family.

items.name: Koutoubia Mosque
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Medina of Marrakesh
items.description: Marrakech's defining silhouette, a 77-metre Almohad minaret from the 1190s that no building in the old city is allowed to rise above. Non-Muslims cannot enter, but the floodlit gardens and evening call to prayer make it the most photographed landmark in the city.

items.name: Bahia Palace
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Medina of Marrakesh
items.description: A late-19th-century grand-vizier's palace of 150-plus rooms threaded around cool courtyards, painted cedar ceilings and orange-tree gardens, the finest example of intact Moroccan craftsmanship in the medina. A private guide brings the harem quarters and zellige to life; go early to have the courtyards nearly to yourself.

items.name: El Badi Palace
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Medina of Marrakesh
items.description: The roofless ruin of Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur's 16th-century 'Incomparable' palace, sunken orange gardens, colossal walls and resident storks nesting on the ramparts. From the rooftop you get one of the best panoramas over the medina to the Atlas.

items.name: Ben Youssef Madrasa
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Medina of Marrakesh
items.description: Once North Africa's largest Islamic college, reopened in 2022 after a meticulous restoration, a jewel-box of carved cedar, stucco and zellige around a still reflecting pool. The quietest, most contemplative of the great medina monuments; unforgettable in early-morning light.

items.name: Saadian Tombs
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Medina of Marrakesh
items.description: The dynastic mausoleum of the Saadian sultans, sealed and forgotten for centuries until rediscovered in 1917, the Chamber of the Twelve Columns, in Carrara marble and gilded honeycomb muqarnas, is a masterpiece. Small and often busy, so a private early slot with a guide is worth arranging.

items.name: Dar Si Said Museum (National Museum of Weaving and Carpets)
items.description: A serene 19th-century riad-palace now devoted to Moroccan weaving and Berber carpets, with woodwork rivalling the Bahia next door. A calm, cultured hour for collectors and anyone who wants the language of tribal rugs before they shop the souks.

items.name: Dar El Bacha, Musée des Confluences
items.description: The restored 1910 palace of the pasha of Marrakech, showcasing craftsmanship and cross-cultural artefacts; its Bacha Coffee room is a destination in itself. Refined, uncrowded and a natural pairing with an unhurried mint-tea stop.

items.name: Maison de la Photographie
items.description: A three-storey riad displaying vintage photographs of Morocco from 1870 to 1950, Berber life, kasbahs and desert caravans. Its rooftop café is one of the highest in the medina, a gentle spot for lunch with sweeping views to the Atlas.

items.name: Marrakech Museum (Musée de Marrakech)
items.description: Housed in the opulent Dar Menebhi Palace, its immense central atrium and chandelier make the architecture as much the draw as the rotating exhibits of Moroccan art. A cool, easy stop steps from Ben Youssef.

items.name: The Souks (Souk Semmarine & the artisan quarters)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Medina of Marrakesh
items.description: The labyrinth north of Jemaa el-Fnaa, organised by craft, babouche slippers, lanterns, leather, carpets and spices. A trusted private guide turns a chaotic maze into an easy, no-pressure afternoon, and can arrange discreet delivery of larger purchases to your riad.

items.name: Le Jardin Secret
items.description: A restored Saadian-era riad garden hidden in the souks, Islamic and exotic gardens divided by water channels, with a tower for rooftop views. A rare pocket of calm and shade in the heart of the medina, lovely for grandparents who need a rest between sights.

items.name: Musée des Tissages / Fondation Montresso and the Mellah
items.description: The 16th-century Jewish quarter, its restored lanes, the Lazama Synagogue and the atmospheric Miaara cemetery telling a quieter chapter of the city's history. Less frantic than the main souks and rich for a guide-led walk into Marrakech's multi-faith past.

items.name: Jardin Majorelle
items.description: The cobalt-blue villa and garden painter Jacques Majorelle created in the 1920s, later rescued by Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé, bamboo, cactus and that unmistakable 'Majorelle blue'. Book the first-entry slot to beat the crowds; the on-site Berber Museum is a small gem.

items.name: Musée Yves Saint Laurent Marrakech
items.description: A striking terracotta-brick museum beside the Majorelle Garden, dedicated to four decades of the designer's haute couture, with an auditorium, library and terrace café. Essential for design-minded travellers and a natural pairing with the garden next door.

items.name: MACAAL (Museum of African Contemporary Art Al Maaden)
items.description: One of Africa's leading privately funded contemporary-art museums, with painting, sculpture, video and photography from across the continent. A serious cultural counterpoint to the historic medina, out by the golf district on the city's edge.

items.name: MACMA (Museum of Art and Culture of Marrakech)
items.description: An intimate private museum in the new town tracing Orientalist painting, vintage photography and Moroccan artefacts. Small, well-curated and easy to fold into a Gueliz gallery afternoon.

items.name: Galerie 127
items.description: Founded in 2006, one of the first galleries in the Arab world dedicated to fine-art photography, showing contemporary Moroccan and international work. A quiet, collector-grade stop for those who want art beyond the souvenir trail.

items.name: Menara Gardens
items.description: A vast 12th-century olive grove around a still reservoir, with the Atlas snow reflected behind a green-tiled pavilion, Marrakech's classic postcard. Peaceful at sunset and a gentle outing away from the medina bustle.

items.name: Agdal Gardens
items.description: One of the oldest gardens in the world, a 12th-century royal orchard of nearly 1,000 acres laid in geometric groves fed by ancient irrigation basins. Vast and historic; opening depends on royal use, so confirm access before setting out.

items.name: ANIMA Garden by André Heller
items.description: The Austrian artist André Heller's surreal botanical garden about 30 minutes out toward the Atlas foothills, cacti, palms, contemporary sculpture and a Paul Bowles-inspired café. A whimsical half-day the whole family enjoys, with a shuttle from the city.

items.name: Le Spa de La Mamounia
items.description: A 2,500-square-metre spa inside Marrakech's most storied hotel, with traditional and private hammams, a heated indoor pool and a jacuzzi pavilion beneath mashrabiya screens. The definitive grande-dame hammam ritual; private suites suit couples and multi-generational bookings.

items.name: Spa at Royal Mansour Marrakech
items.description: A soaring 27,000-square-foot wellness palace of white filigree, with 13 treatment rooms, a Watsu pool and a signature hammam where a musician sings as your mask sets. Regularly rated among the world's finest spas, the most discreet, private luxury ritual in the city.

items.name: Les Bains de Marrakech
items.description: A long-established medina hammam and spa offering the full gommage-and-black-soap ritual in candlelit settings, with private cabins available. A more traditional, atmospheric counterpoint to the palace spas, and easy to book without staying in-house.

items.name: La Maison Arabe Cooking Workshop
items.description: The city's most famous cooking school, run by a dada (traditional Moroccan cook) with a translator, including a spice-market visit and communal bread oven. Vegetarian tagines and couscous are readily accommodated, a hands-on afternoon that travels well across generations.

items.name: Amal Women's Training Center, Lunch & Cooking Class
items.description: A non-profit restaurant and school that trains disadvantaged women, serving a superb daily home-style lunch and morning cooking classes. Warm, purposeful and deeply local, the kind of meaningful, values-led experience discerning travellers remember most.

items.name: Rooftop dinner at Nomad
items.description: A modern-Moroccan rooftop above the spice square, serving lighter, contemporary takes on the classics with strong vegetarian options and skyline views. A relaxed, design-forward evening in the heart of the old city, easy to book for a family table.

items.name: Dinner at Le Grand Café de la Poste
items.description: A restored 1920s colonial-era brasserie in the new town, all palms, ceiling fans and Art Deco, for a French-Moroccan menu away from the medina crush. A calm, elegant option for an evening when you want tablecloths and quiet conversation.

items.name: Afternoon tea at La Mamounia
items.description: The ritual of mint tea and Moroccan pastries in the gardens or grand salons of the city's legendary hotel, a Churchill-era institution. A polished, air-conditioned pause that grandparents and children both enjoy between sightseeing.

items.name: Rooftop tea at a medina riad
items.description: The quintessential Marrakech ritual, mint tea and stillness on a tiled rooftop as the Koutoubia and Atlas glow at golden hour. A private riad or a rooftop café such as those above Dar El Bacha or the Mellah makes for the most discreet version.

items.name: The Tanneries of Marrakech
items.description: The centuries-old open-air pits near Bab Debbagh where hides are still cured by hand in the traditional way, pungent, raw and endlessly photographed from the surrounding terraces. Go with a reputable guide to avoid touts, and be ready for the smell (mint sprig in hand).

items.name: Ensemble Artisanal
items.description: A government-run artisan complex where craftsmen work at fixed, honest prices, leather, metal, textiles and ceramics without the haggling of the souks. A calm, no-pressure place to understand quality before buying, ideal for first-time or time-pressed shoppers.

items.name: Ceramics and pottery at the Bab Ghmat / Sidi Ghanem quarters
items.description: Sidi Ghanem is the design district where Marrakech's serious ceramic, tadelakt and homeware ateliers and concept stores cluster, supplying riads and hotels worldwide. Off the tourist map and perfect for collectors sourcing tableware and tiles at the source.

items.name: Camel ride in the Palmeraie
items.description: A gentle hour on camelback through the palm groves on the city's northern edge, a soft, scenic introduction to the desert without the long drive. Easygoing enough for children and grandparents, and often paired with tea in a Berber tent.

items.name: Quad biking in the Palmeraie
items.description: Guided quad-bike circuits through the palm groves and rocky tracks north of the city for those wanting a shot of adrenaline close to base. A fun half-day for teenagers and active travellers, easily arranged privately.

items.name: Hot-air balloon flight over the Palmeraie and Atlas foothills
items.description: A dawn balloon drifting over palm groves, Berber villages and the snow-capped High Atlas, usually followed by a desert breakfast. A once-in-a-trip, weather-permitting experience that private operators can tailor to a small group.

items.name: Golf at Royal Golf de Marrakech / Amelkis / Al Maaden
items.description: Marrakech's championship courses lie in palm and olive country with the Atlas as backdrop, the Royal Golf dates to the 1920s and hosted royalty and Churchill. A relaxed day for golfing members of the party while others explore the city.

items.name: Musée Boucharouite
items.description: A small, personal museum devoted to boucharouite, the vibrant recycled-rag rugs of rural Morocco, inside a restored medina house. A quiet, off-beat stop that textile lovers adore and few tourists find.

items.name: Le Jardin des Arts / private galleries of Gueliz
items.description: A cluster of commercial galleries and design boutiques in the new town showing contemporary Moroccan painters, photographers and sculptors. An easy afternoon of collecting and coffee, well away from the medina's intensity.

items.name: Imlil and the High Atlas
items.description: The Berber village at the foot of Mount Toubkal, North Africa's highest peak, walnut groves, terraced fields and a gateway to gentle valley walks or serious trekking. A private guide and 4x4 make a comfortable day; the Kasbah du Toubkal offers a spectacular lunch stop with a view.

items.name: Ourika Valley
items.description: A green river valley climbing into the Atlas, riverside Berber cafés, waterfalls at Setti Fatma and cooler mountain air an hour from the city. An easy, scenic escape from summer heat, and family-friendly with a private car and guide.

items.name: Agafay Desert
items.description: A lunar expanse of rolling stone desert under an hour from the city, with the snow-capped Atlas on the horizon, luxury camps, camel rides, sunset dinners and stargazing without the long Sahara drive. The most convenient 'desert' experience, and easily done as a private day or overnight.

items.name: Essaouira
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Medina of Essaouira (formerly Mogador)
items.description: The breezy, walled fishing port on the Atlantic, a UNESCO-listed medina of white-and-blue lanes, art galleries, fresh seafood grills and Game-of-Thrones ramparts. A cooling coastal contrast to the red city; comfortable as a long private day or a relaxed overnight.

items.name: Ouzoud Falls
items.description: Morocco's most dramatic waterfalls, a 110-metre triple cascade framed by red cliffs and olive groves, with wild Barbary macaques and boat rides at the base. A spectacular full-day outing best done privately to avoid the coach crowds.

items.name: Sunset cocktails and dinner at a Palmeraie country retreat
items.description: The palm-grove belt north of the city holds discreet country hotels and clubs where an evening of poolside drinks and dinner under the palms feels a world from the medina. A refined, private way to end a day, easily arranged through your riad or advisor.

items.name: Guided medina walking tour with a licensed historian
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Medina of Marrakesh
items.description: Marrakech's old city rewards a knowledgeable private guide who can read its palaces, fondouks and craft quarters, and keep touts and wrong turns at bay. The single best investment for a first visit, turning a bewildering maze into a coherent, comfortable story.

items.name: La Grande Table Marocaine
credentials: MENA's 50 Best Restaurants No. 19 (2026), Art of Hospitality Award
items.description: Moroccan haute cuisine at its very summit, spice-packed sh'hiwates, seafood pastilla and seven-vegetable couscous, immaculately staged.

items.name: Sesamo
items.description: Massimiliano Alajmo's Italian at the Royal Mansour, the 'Mozart of Italian cuisine', translated to Morocco.

items.name: Le Marocain
items.description: A One Thousand and One Nights dining room, Chef Rachid Agouray's Moroccan cooking, an institution for thirty years.

items.name: L'Italien par Jean-Georges
items.description: Jean-Georges Vongerichten's Italian inside the Grande Dame, refined, sunlit and faultlessly served.

items.name: Le Petit Cornichon
items.description: Chef Erwann Lance, schooled by Ripert and Alléno, brings bistronomy to Marrakech, French classics with a Moroccan hand.
Relaxed, sun-drenched Australian cooking, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and South Asian flavours, everything made in-house.

items.name: Farmers
items.description: Season-led, permaculture-farm cooking in a restored Art Deco gallery, the most talked-about opening in the city.

items.name: La Grande Brasserie by Hélène Darroze
credentials: Restaurant of a World's 50 Best Hotel (Royal Mansour, No. 13, 2025)
items.description: Hélène Darroze's French brasserie at the Royal Mansour, warm, produce-led cooking from a three-star chef.

items.name: Le Jardin (Royal Mansour)
credentials: Restaurant of a World's 50 Best Hotel (Royal Mansour, No. 13, 2025)
items.description: Mediterranean cooking under the Royal Mansour's greenery, bright, garden-fresh, unhurried.

items.name: Dar Yacout
items.description: A candlelit palace dinner, the theatrical, multi-course Moroccan feast Marrakech is romanced for.

items.name: Dar Moha
items.description: Moroccan gastronomy in Pierre Bergé's former riad, poolside, refined, and quietly pioneering.

items.name: Nobu Marrakech
credentials: Restaurant of a Small Luxury Hotel (Nobu Hotel Marrakech)
items.description: The global Nobu template restaged in Morocco, black cod, new-style sashimi, with a rooftop over the city.

items.name: Rivayat
credentials: Restaurant of a MICHELIN Two-Key hotel (The Oberoi Marrakech, 2025)
items.description: Award-winning Indian cooking from a Michelin-starred chef, in the Oberoi's palace of olive groves.

items.name: L'Italien par Simone Zanoni
credentials: Restaurant of a World's 50 Best / MICHELIN Three-Key hotel (La Mamounia)
items.description: A luxury trattoria within La Mamounia, wood-fired pizza and pasta from a Ducasse-schooled chef.

items.name: Nomad
items.description: Modern Moroccan over four floors of an old carpet store, fresh, local and with the best Medina-and-Atlas rooftop view.

items.name: Al Fassia
items.description: The women-run Fassi kitchen that has defined home-style Moroccan cooking in the city for decades.

items.name: Le Trou au Mur
items.description: Forgotten Moroccan home recipes revived with real care, the domestic cooking few restaurants bother with.

items.name: El Fenn Restaurant
credentials: Restaurant of a Condé Nast-recommended riad (El Fenn)
items.description: Mediterranean-Moroccan cooking in the city's most photogenic riad, colour, courtyards and a legendary roof.

items.name: Bistrot Amaia
items.description: A French-Moroccan neighbourhood bistrot doing careful, market-led cooking away from the tourist beat.

items.name: Café Clock
items.description: A cultural café as much as a kitchen, the famous camel burger, storytelling nights and young Marrakech.

items.name: Le Churchill Bar
credentials: Bar of a World's 50 Best / MICHELIN Three-Key hotel (La Mamounia)
items.description: Dark wood, deep leather and cigars, the legendary bar named for Marrakech's most famous guest, in its grandest hotel.

items.name: Baromètre
credentials: Widely cited as Marrakech's leading cocktail bar
items.description: A speakeasy of vintage-laboratory theatre and house infusions, the city's most serious mixology, hidden in Gueliz.

items.name: Le Bar Italien / Le Grand Bar
credentials: Bar of a World's 50 Best / MICHELIN Three-Key hotel (La Mamounia)
items.description: La Mamounia's glamorous salon bars, live music, a dressed crowd and cocktails with a Pierre Hermé finish.

items.name: El Fenn Rooftop
credentials: Rooftop of a Condé Nast-recommended riad (El Fenn)
items.description: Bohemian colour and cushions above the Medina, the Koutoubia minaret catching the last of the sun, the sunset drink everyone chases.

items.name: Nobu Rooftop Bar
credentials: Rooftop of a Small Luxury Hotel (Nobu Hotel Marrakech)
items.description: Sleek, DJ-driven and international, cocktails over a lit-up city from Nobu's circular rooftop pool deck.

plan.heading: 4 days in Marrakech, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into La Mamounia or a private Royal Mansour riad, then a late-morning tea in the garden.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Bahia Palace and the Saadian Tombs with a guide, then the tanners' and dyers' souks at an unhurried pace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Le Grand Restaurant Français within La Mamounia, or the courtyard of Dar Yacout.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Jardin Majorelle and the Yves Saint Laurent Museum at opening, before the tour groups.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Menara gardens and a hammam and rest at the hotel spa through the afternoon heat.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at +61 or the Moroccan tasting menu at Le Jardin, in a lantern-lit courtyard.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A drive into the High Atlas to the Kasbah du Toubkal, tea with a Berber family in a village.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A gentle walk among the terraced valleys, then lunch on a mountain terrace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to the city for dinner at the elegant, hushed Al Fassia, run entirely by women.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Ben Youssef Madrasa and Le Jardin Secret before the square wakes.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A cooking lesson or simply the Palmeraie by horse, then a poolside afternoon.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last dinner at the Royal Mansour's La Grande Table Marocaine, followed by the square at night from a rooftop.

items.name: The Medina
items.description: Inside the walls among the souks and the Jemaa el-Fnaa, atmospheric riad living, best for those who want to be in the thick of it.

items.name: Hivernage
items.description: The wide, modern quarter of large hotels, spas and restaurants; suits travellers who prefer space, pools and easy arrivals.

items.name: The Palmeraie
items.description: The palm-grove belt outside town of private estates and resorts; for a calm, low-rise base with day-trips into the medina.

events.name: Marrakech Comedy Festival (Marrakech du Rire)
events.note: The city's headline comedy weekend, now under a new name and home at the Palais des Congrès.

events.name: Marrakech International Film Festival
events.note: The prestige film festival that brings international directors and stars to the Palais Badii and the medina squares.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in a restored riad inside the medina for atmosphere or La Mamounia for grandeur; dress modestly, expect persistent souk vendors, and let your riad arrange guides to avoid the touts.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Marrakech Menara (RAK), ten minutes from the medina; a private car meets you, and a riad will send a porter to walk your bags the final lanes cars cannot enter.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The medina is a warren best explored on foot with a guide, while a private driver handles the Palmeraie, the Atlas foothills, and dinner beyond the walls.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Maroc Telecom, Orange) is reliable; riad and hotel wifi is standard, though thick medina walls can dampen signal.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Moroccan dirham (MAD) is a closed currency, draw it locally; cards work in hotels and finer restaurants, cash rules the souks, and 10% or rounding up is expected.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: March-May and mid-September-November are the sweet spots, warm days, cool riad evenings; July-August pushes past 40°C, and midwinter nights get genuinely cold.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India; Royal Air Maroc connects via Casablanca, or route one-stop on a Gulf carrier (Emirates/Qatar) or via Paris on Air France, roughly 12-15 hours total. The Gulf and Paris routings offer stronger business cabins; a Casablanca connection is the shortest onward hop to Marrakech.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No special vaccinations beyond routine; current hepatitis A and typhoid advisable. Bottled water for drinking. Safe overall; the medina's souks bring persistent touts and hustle, a good private guide removes most of it, and ordinary care against pickpockets applies.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Good for vegetarians, vegetable tagines, couscous, salads and breads are everywhere; Jain needs briefing on onion/garlic and stock. Indian food is limited, but the top riads and hotels (La Mamounia, Royal Mansour) will prepare refined vegetarian and Indian-inflected menus to order.
